text: Ever drank an icy slushie and felt an ice pick stab your forehead?
That agonizing headache isn't in your brain at all.
When ice touches the roof of your mouth, the sudden freezing temperature triggers an emergency survival reflex.
To protect your brain from freezing, your body rapidly constricts the anterior cerebral artery, then violently floods it with warm blood.
Your trigeminal nerve detects this sudden blood surge, but it gets confused.
Because this nerve also connects to your forehead, your brain assumes your face is in danger, creating intense referred pain.
To stop it instantly, press your warm tongue against the roof of your mouth.
The heat relaxes the artery, silencing the alarm before you ask...
